gemini.depth_why: The scenery changes with the seasons, from winter snow and road closures to lush summer coasts and vibrant fall foliage.
gemini.overview: Acadia National Park is defined by its rugged Atlantic coastline, where granite cliffs meet the ocean. Visitors drive or hike to the summit of Cadillac Mountain for sweeping views of the islands and sea, or walk the carriage roads around Jordan Pond. The scenery peaks in October when the forests turn bright red and gold.

blurbs.text: Most of the Park Loop Road is closed to cars, but the snow-covered granite shores and frozen lakes offer quiet, stark coastal views for those on foot or skis.
Melting snow and spring rain fill the streams, and the forests begin to green. The Park Loop Road fully reopens by mid-April, restoring easy access to the major viewpoints.
The coastal views are clear and the forests are lush. The drive up Cadillac Mountain and the trails around Jordan Pond are fully accessible, showing off the rocky shores and deep blue water.

The landscape transforms as the hardwood forests turn vibrant shades of orange, red, and yellow. The contrast of the autumn foliage against the dark granite cliffs and the ocean makes this the most striking time to see the park.
The autumn leaves have fallen, leaving the forests bare. The scenery is muted, and late in the month, sections of the main park roads close for the winter season.

gemini.depth_why: The coastal cliffs and sea stacks are permanent rock formations.
gemini.overview: The Algarve is defined by its Atlantic coastline of steep limestone cliffs, enclosed coves, and golden rock formations. The sea stacks and arches of Ponta da Piedade rise directly from the water, creating a maze of stone pillars. Nearby, the Benagil cave features a natural oculus that frames the sky above an interior beach.

blurbs.text: The limestone cliffs and sea stacks stand fully visible, with coastal trails offering clear vantage points over the Atlantic. Boat and kayak routes to the sea caves operate when ocean swells permit, and the rock formations can always be seen from the headlands above.

gemini.depth_why: Scores peak in spring for the bulb fields, while the rest of the year is grouped by daylight hours for viewing the canals.
gemini.overview: Amsterdam's scenery is defined by water, with a vast network of historic canals shaping the city center. Beyond the urban waterways, the surrounding flatlands transform in spring when massive fields of tulips and other bulbs bloom in bright, geometric stripes. The most distinct views are found along the canal rings at dusk or in the countryside during the spring bloom.

blurbs.text: Short winter days mean the sun sets early, but the canal rings remain the focal point of the landscape. The waterways reflect the lights of the bridges in the early evenings, and occasional winter frosts can leave a thin layer of ice on the smaller canals.

Millions of tulips, daffodils, and hyacinths bloom in the fields just outside the city, creating vast stripes of bright color across the flat landscape. The canal rings are lined with budding trees, and lengthening days provide more time for evening walks along the water.

Long summer evenings and mild autumn days leave plenty of daylight to take in the canal rings. The water reflects the historic bridges and tall, narrow houses, while the trees lining the waterways turn from deep green to autumn gold by late October.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise in spring and early summer when the landscape is greenest, dip slightly in the heat of late summer, and fall in winter.
gemini.overview: The region's signature views blend dramatic natural settings with historic architecture, most famously the Alhambra against the Sierra Nevada and the deep gorge splitting Ronda. The landscape ranges from the rugged southern coast to arid badlands and rolling hills dotted with whitewashed villages. Spring and early summer offer the clearest skies and greenest hillsides before the intense heat of late summer dries the terrain.

blurbs.text: Winter brings cooler temperatures and occasional rain, turning the hillsides green. The Sierra Nevada mountains are often capped with snow, providing a striking backdrop to the Alhambra, though some higher mountain passes may be closed.

The hills and valleys are at their greenest, and the weather is clear for driving the routes between the whitewashed villages. The coastal cliffs and the deep El Tajo gorge in Ronda are easily accessible before the peak summer heat arrives.

The landscape dries out under intense sun, turning the rolling hills golden and brown. The arid badlands of the Tabernas Desert look their most stark, while the coastal views remain clear, though the heat makes long walks less comfortable.

gemini.depth_why: Scores fall into three distinct seasons based on the monsoon cycle and visibility.
gemini.overview: Cambodia's scenery is defined by the jungle reclaiming ancient stone and the vast floodplains of the Mekong River. The signature views are the massive strangler figs overtaking the ruins of Ta Prohm and the silhouette of Angkor Wat at sunrise. Beyond the temple complexes, the landscape features flat rice paddies, the dense forests of the Cardamom Mountains, and the seasonal swelling of Tonle Sap lake.

blurbs.text: Clear skies provide the best conditions for the famous sunrise behind Angkor Wat. The countryside is still relatively green from the recent rains, and dry dirt roads make it easy to reach remote jungle temples and the Cardamom Mountains.

The dry season peaks, turning the rice paddies and rural landscapes brown and dusty. Agricultural burning often creates a haze that washes out the sky and obscures distant views, though the jungle around Ta Prohm remains shaded.

Monsoon rains transform the country into a vibrant, lush green and swell the waters of Tonle Sap lake. Heavy cloud cover frequently blocks sunrises, and frequent downpours turn unpaved rural routes into thick mud, limiting access to remote areas.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with access and visibility due to winter snow and summer heat.
gemini.overview: The draw here is the world-class desert and canyon scenery, defined by thousands of natural sandstone arches, deep gorges, and towering mesas. Delicate Arch at sunset and Mesa Arch at dawn are the signature views, while the Island in the Sky district offers sweeping overlooks of the canyon country. The landscape is best seen in spring and fall, when temperatures allow for longer hikes and drives.

blurbs.text: Winter brings cold temperatures and occasional snow, which can temporarily close roads and trails. The contrast of white snow against red rock is striking, but access to some viewpoints may be limited.
Spring begins to warm the desert, melting the snow and opening up full access to the trails and scenic drives. The views are clear and the landscape is fully accessible.
The weather is ideal for exploring the viewpoints and hiking to the arches. The clear skies and mild temperatures make this the prime time to see the canyons and rock formations.
Summer heat can be intense, making midday hikes to the arches difficult. The scenery remains fully visible, but early morning or late evening visits are necessary to comfortably reach the viewpoints.
Temperatures cool down, bringing back ideal conditions for hiking and driving through the parks. The clear autumn air provides excellent visibility across the vast canyon landscapes.
Late fall and early winter bring colder weather and the possibility of snow. While the main roads usually remain open, some trails to the arches may become icy or harder to reach.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery changes with distinct summer access, autumn colors, winter snow, and spring snowmelt.
gemini.overview: The Argentine Lake District is defined by deep glacial lakes set against the forested peaks of the Andes. The Seven Lakes Road and Circuito Chico drives connect these water bodies, providing continuous views of mountains, rivers and dense forests. The landscape shifts from green valleys to snow-capped summits depending on the elevation.

blurbs.text: Clear roads and dry trails allow full access to high mountain passes and remote lake shores. The long daylight hours provide ample time for driving the major scenic routes.
The lenga and ñire forests turn bright red and yellow, contrasting sharply with the blue lakes. Rain increases late in the season, and low clouds can occasionally obscure the higher peaks.
Snow covers the Andes and lower forests, completely altering the landscape. Shorter days and heavy snowfall restrict access to unpaved scenic routes and higher mountain viewpoints.
Heavy snowmelt swells the region's rivers and waterfalls to their highest volumes. The lower valleys turn green again, though high mountain passes often hold snow until late in the season.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery in Aruba is accessible and largely unchanged throughout the year.
gemini.overview: Aruba's scenery is defined by its coasts, contrasting calm white-sand beaches with a rugged, arid eastern shore. Eagle Beach provides the classic Caribbean view of wide sand and clear water, while Arikok National Park covers much of the island with a dry landscape of cacti and limestone cliffs. The eastern coastline features natural bridges and crashing waves against the rock.

blurbs.text: The coastal views remain clear and accessible. The contrast between the calm western beaches and the rough, cactus-studded eastern shore in Arikok National Park is visible on drives and walks.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with snow cover, access to high passes, and autumn color.
gemini.overview: The Elk Mountains define the scenery here, anchored by the Maroon Bells, two 14,000-foot peaks reflected in a high alpine lake. The surrounding valleys hold dense forests of aspen trees that turn bright gold in autumn. High-elevation drives like Independence Pass offer sweeping views of the peaks and tundra, while winter brings deep snow cover to the slopes.

blurbs.text: Deep snow covers the peaks and valleys, turning the landscape into a winter scene. Independence Pass and the road to the Maroon Bells are closed to cars, but the snow-covered mountains are visible from the ski areas and town.
Snow begins to melt at lower elevations, leaving the landscape in transition. High passes and the road to the Maroon Bells remain closed to vehicles.
Spring green reaches the valleys, though snow remains on the high peaks. Independence Pass and the road to the Maroon Bells typically open late in the month, restoring access to the signature views.
The high country is fully accessible. The Maroon Bells are clear of snow and reflected in the lake, and Independence Pass offers drives above the tree line. The forests are deep green.
The aspen forests turn bright gold, contrasting with the evergreen pines and the gray rock of the peaks. The Maroon Bells and Independence Pass remain open and offer the most vivid views of the year.

The autumn leaves drop early in the month, and the first snows begin to dust the high peaks. The landscape transitions toward winter, and high-elevation roads may close temporarily or for the season depending on storms.

Snow begins to accumulate in the valleys, and the high passes, including Independence Pass and the road to the Maroon Bells, close for the winter. The scenery is stark before the deep winter snowpack builds.

gemini.depth_why: The Altiplanic winter slightly reduces access to high-altitude sites in January and February, separating them from the rest of the year.
gemini.overview: The Atacama Desert holds some of the most extreme arid landscapes on Earth. Visitors come for the jagged, salt-crusted rock formations of Moon Valley and the vast salt flats stretching toward volcanic horizons. High in the Andes, the bright blue Altiplanic lagoons sit beneath snow-capped peaks, while the El Tatio geysers send up thick columns of steam at dawn.

blurbs.text: Summer brings the Altiplanic winter, pulling occasional rain and snow over the high Andes. The moisture can temporarily close dirt roads to the high-altitude lagoons and geysers, though the lower valleys usually remain clear.
Dry, clear conditions keep the high-altitude dirt roads open and the volcanic horizons sharp. The lack of moisture ensures reliable access to the geysers at dawn and the salt flats at sunset.

gemini.depth_why: The urban landscape and iconic views of the Acropolis remain visible in every season.
gemini.overview: The defining landscape of the Greek capital is the Acropolis rising sharply above the dense urban sprawl. Viewpoints like Mount Lycabettus and Philopappos Hill offer sweeping panoramas of the ancient citadel set against the modern city and the distant Aegean Sea. The surrounding Attica region also provides modest coastal scenery along the Saronic Gulf.

blurbs.text: The rocky hills scattered throughout the city provide the best vantage points for taking in the urban landscape. Trails up Mount Lycabettus and Philopappos Hill look directly across to the Parthenon, with the sprawling white buildings of the capital stretching out to the coastline.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise gradually from winter to summer as visibility improves and hydrangeas bloom.
gemini.overview: The Azores are known for volcanic calderas, crater lakes and dramatic green coastlines. The signature views are the twin lakes of Sete Cidades and the caldera of Lagoa do Fogo on São Miguel. Summer brings the best visibility and the famous blue hydrangeas that line the roads, particularly on Faial.

blurbs.text: Winter brings frequent rain, low clouds and fog that can obscure the higher viewpoints, including the crater lakes. The coastal scenery remains visible, though the seas are often rough.
Spring sees improving visibility and longer days for driving the coastal routes. The landscape turns bright green, and the first hydrangeas begin to bloom late in the season.
Summer offers the clearest skies for viewing the calderas and lakes from high vantage points. Blue hydrangeas are in full bloom along the roadsides and coastal cliffs.
Autumn brings a return of low clouds and increasing rain, which can hide the mountain viewpoints. The waterfalls run fuller after the rains begin.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change as snow closes high-elevation scenic drives in winter and clears for full access in summer.
gemini.overview: The region contrasts the sharply eroded, banded buttes of the Badlands with the dark, pine-covered granite peaks of the Black Hills. Scenic drives such as the Needles Highway and Badlands Loop Road navigate narrow rock tunnels, steep canyons, and vast prairie overlooks. The landscapes range from dry, colorful desert pinnacles to dense mountain forests.

blurbs.text: Snow often closes high-elevation routes in the Black Hills, including the Needles Highway and Iron Mountain Road. The Badlands Loop Road usually remains plowed, showing the eroded desert pinnacles dusted in white.
Thawing clears the lower canyon roads, and the high granite passes in the Black Hills begin to reopen for driving.
All scenic routes are clear, allowing drives through the narrow rock tunnels of the Needles Highway and full access to the vast desert overlooks of the Badlands.
Autumn brings yellow foliage to the canyons of the Black Hills before early snows start to limit access to the highest mountain passes.

gemini.depth_why: Scores follow the dry and wet seasons, with visibility and access dropping during the monsoon.
gemini.overview: The signature view of Myanmar is the plain of Bagan, where thousands of ancient temples rise from the dust, often seen at sunrise from a hot air balloon. Beyond the temples, the landscape is defined by the Irrawaddy River, the floating villages and leg-rowers of Inle Lake, and the limestone karst formations of Hpa-An. The scenery is best viewed during the dry, cooler months when skies are clear.

blurbs.text: Clear skies and dry weather make this the prime time to see the temples of Bagan at sunrise, with hot air balloons operating daily. The waters of Inle Lake are calm, and the views of the surrounding hills and floating gardens are sharp.

Heat builds across the plains, creating hazy conditions that can soften the views of the temples and the Irrawaddy River. Hot air balloon flights over Bagan typically end their season as temperatures rise.
The monsoon begins, bringing heavy rains and thick cloud cover that obscure the hills and temples. Dirt roads in rural areas become muddy, making access to some viewpoints difficult.
Heavy monsoon rains peak, washing out rural roads and keeping skies overcast. Visibility is low, and the Irrawaddy River swells, changing the landscape but making travel to viewpoints challenging.

The rains begin to ease, leaving the countryside lush and green. The skies slowly clear, and hot air balloon flights over Bagan usually resume toward the end of this period as the dry season approaches.

gemini.depth_why: Scores drop during the wet and hurricane seasons as clouds and storms reduce water clarity.
gemini.overview: The Bahamas is defined by its coastal scenery, where shallow sandbanks create distinctive turquoise and sapphire waters. The Exuma chain offers hundreds of small cays and sandbars, including the well-known beach at Big Major Cay. The clearest views and most vivid water colors align with the dry season.

blurbs.text: Clear skies and calm conditions maximize water clarity, making the shallow banks and cays highly visible. The vivid blues of the ocean contrast sharply with the white sandbars.
Humidity rises and brief showers become more common, slightly softening the horizon. The water remains mostly clear for viewing the cays.
Summer brings heavier rain showers and building clouds that can cast shadows over the shallow banks, dulling the water's color.
Tropical storms and heavy rain are most frequent, often churning up the sand and reducing water clarity. Overcast skies frequently mute the contrast between the ocean and the islands.
Storm risks fade and the skies begin to clear. The water settles, returning the sharp turquoise colors to the coastal views.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with the transition between the cloudy wet season and the clear dry season.
gemini.overview: Bali is defined by its steep coastal cliffs and terraced inland forests. Visitors can walk the green steps of the Tegallalang rice terraces or look out over the ocean from the limestone drops at Uluwatu. Inland, the volcanic cone of Mount Batur rises above a crater lake, surrounded by jungle waterfalls and river gorges.

blurbs.text: Heavy rains and low clouds frequently obscure the volcanic peaks and coastal horizons. Trails around the crater lakes become muddy, and runoff can cloud the coastal waters, though the inland rice terraces remain bright green.

The rains ease and the skies clear, revealing sharper views of the inland volcanoes and coastal drops. The forests and terraces are lush from the recent wet months, making this a strong window for photography before the driest conditions set in.

Clear, dry skies provide the sharpest visibility for sunrise hikes up Mount Batur and long views down the Uluwatu cliffs. The coastal waters appear bright blue against the limestone, and the jungle trails to inland waterfalls are firm and accessible.

Cloud cover begins to build over the central mountains as the dry conditions end. The coastal cliffs still offer clear sightlines over the water, but afternoon haze often softens the views of the inland valleys and crater lakes.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery changes with the freezing and thawing of the lakes and the seasonal closure of high-elevation roads.
gemini.overview: The Canadian Rockies present massive limestone peaks, deep valleys, and expansive icefields. Visitors drive the Icefields Parkway to see glaciers and dense pine forests, or walk the shores of Moraine Lake and Lake Louise to view their bright turquoise waters. The scenery is most accessible and the lakes are fully thawed from June through September.

blurbs.text: Snow covers the peaks and pine forests, and the famous lakes freeze over entirely. The road to Moraine Lake is closed to vehicles, but the Icefields Parkway remains open for winter driving past frozen waterfalls and glaciers.

The lower valleys begin to thaw, though the major lakes often remain frozen into late May. Snow still blocks higher trails and viewpoints, but the melting ice creates heavy flow in the rivers and waterfalls.

The lakes melt completely, revealing the bright blue glacial rock flour that makes Lake Louise and Moraine Lake famous. All high-elevation roads are open for driving, and the glaciers along the Icefields Parkway are clearly visible.
Snow begins to accumulate on the mountains again, and the lakes start to freeze. The access road to Moraine Lake typically closes to vehicles in the middle of the month as winter conditions set in.

gemini.depth_why: The urban riverfront scenery and river access do not change with the months.
gemini.overview: The primary view in Bangkok is the wide Chao Phraya River flowing past the city's temples and high-rises. The signature sight is Wat Arun illuminated at dusk across the water. The surrounding landscape is a flat river plain, leaving the urban skyline and the active waterways as the main visual draws.

blurbs.text: The Chao Phraya River serves as the focal point for scenery, with ferries and longtail boats navigating the water. Dusk offers clear views of Wat Arun and the illuminated skyline from the riverbanks.

gemini.depth_why: The coastal scenery does not change across the months.
gemini.overview: Barbados is defined by its coastal scenery, with a sharp contrast between its eastern and western shores. The Atlantic side features the rugged, rock-strewn beaches of Bathsheba, where heavy surf shapes the limestone formations. On the west coast, calmer waters meet flat stretches of sand.

blurbs.text: The Atlantic surf continually batters the eastern limestone rocks at Bathsheba, shaping the rugged shoreline. On the opposite side of the island, the western beaches offer flat stretches of sand and calm water.

gemini.na_reason: City beauty belongs to Architecture and City Exploration.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise steadily toward a clear summer peak for coastal visibility, creating distinct seasonal groups.
gemini.overview: The Basque Country is defined by its dramatic coastline, where green hills drop into the Bay of Biscay. The standout sights are the sweeping crescent of San Sebastián's La Concha bay and the jagged rock formations of the Flysch coast. Inland, modest forested mountains and traditional villages offer quieter rural views.

blurbs.text: Winter brings frequent rain and low clouds that obscure the coastal hills. The rough seas create dramatic waves against the Flysch cliffs, though shorter days limit time for coastal walks.
Spring clears much of the winter fog, revealing bright green hillsides along the coast. The lengthening days provide ample time to drive the coastal roads and walk the cliff paths.
Clear skies and long daylight hours offer the best visibility for the region's signature coastal views. The waters of La Concha bay appear bright blue against the surrounding green peaks.
Autumn introduces more clouds and rain, softening the light over the coastal cliffs. The inland forests take on muted fall colors before the heavier winter weather sets in.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise through spring to a summer peak, then fall through autumn to a winter low.
gemini.overview: Bavaria is defined by the Bavarian Alps and the deep, clear lakes that sit below them. The signature view is Neuschwanstein Castle set against the mountains, while Lake Königssee offers steep, fjord-like shores. Forests and rolling hills cover much of the region, with viewpoints accessible by cable car or mountain road. The scenery is best seen from late spring to early autumn, when high trails and passes are clear of snow.

blurbs.text: Snow covers the Alps and higher elevations, closing many mountain passes and high hiking trails. The lakes and lower valleys remain visible, often under a layer of snow, and cable cars run for winter sports, though daylight is short.
Snow begins to melt in the valleys, revealing green meadows, though the higher peaks and passes remain snowbound. Waterfalls run high with the meltwater, and lower trails open up.

The high Alpine passes, including the Rossfeld Panoramastrasse, are fully open. Trails around Lake Königssee and the viewpoints above Neuschwanstein Castle are clear, and the forests are deep green. Summer brings the longest daylight for driving the scenic routes.
Autumn color peaks in the mixed forests of the lower Alps and around the lakes. The high passes and cable cars generally remain open, though early snow can occasionally dust the highest peaks.

gemini.depth_why: Scores vary by season, peaking in autumn when visibility is best and foliage turns, with lower scores in winter due to cold and haze.
gemini.overview: The primary scenic draw here is the Great Wall, which snakes across the rugged Yanshan mountains north of the city. Sections like Mutianyu and Jiankou offer sweeping views of the stone fortifications following the steep ridges and plunging into the valleys. Within the city, the vast scale of the Forbidden City and the hilltop pavilions of Jingshan Park provide striking urban vistas. The surrounding hills are heavily forested, turning vibrant colors in the autumn.

blurbs.text: Winter brings cold, dry air and occasional snow that dusts the mountains and the Great Wall. Haze and smog can sometimes obscure the longer views, but clear days offer stark, leafless vistas of the rugged terrain.

Spring warms the region, and the forests around the Great Wall begin to green. Peach and apricot blossoms appear on the hillsides, softening the rocky landscapes, though spring winds can occasionally bring dust.
The mountains are lush and fully green, providing a vibrant contrast to the stone of the Great Wall. Visibility is generally good before the heavier summer rains arrive.
Summer is the wet season, bringing frequent rain and high humidity. The forests are at their thickest, but low clouds and summer haze can sometimes limit the sweeping views from the higher ridges.

Autumn offers the clearest skies and the sharpest views of the mountains and the city. The forests around the Great Wall turn bright shades of red and gold, making the hikes along the ridges particularly striking.

The autumn colors fade and the trees lose their leaves as the air turns sharply colder. Visibility remains mostly clear before the winter haze settles in, offering unobstructed views of the mountain contours.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise and fall with daylight and weather, peaking in summer when coastal views are clearest.
gemini.overview: Northern Ireland's scenery is defined by its dramatic coastline, anchored by the Giant's Causeway and its thousands of interlocking basalt columns. The Causeway Coastal Route traces the edge of the country, passing sea cliffs, ruined castles and sweeping glens. Inland, the landscape softens into rolling green hills and quiet forests, including the tunnel of beech trees known as the Dark Hedges.

blurbs.text: Short days and frequent rain limit time for coastal drives and walks. The Giant's Causeway and the Dark Hedges are quiet, but low clouds and storms often obscure the sea views along the northern cliffs.
Spring brings longer daylight for driving the Causeway Coastal Route. The glens and hills turn bright green, though rain and wind are still common along the exposed coast.

Long summer days provide the best conditions for exploring the coast. The basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway and the sea cliffs are clearest, and the extended twilight allows for late-evening drives along the northern shore.
Autumn brings changing colors to the inland glens and the Dark Hedges. The coast remains accessible, but daylight shortens quickly and storms begin to roll in off the Atlantic.

gemini.depth_why: Visibility for aerial views and access to forest roads change with the wet and dry seasons.
gemini.overview: The primary scenic draw is the coastline, defined by the barrier reef cayes and the deep marine sinkhole of the Great Blue Hole seen from the air. Inland, the landscape transitions to dense tropical forests and modest mountain ridges. Clear skies and calm waters from late winter through spring provide the best visibility for aerial flights and boat trips.

blurbs.text: Clear skies and calm waters maximize visibility for aerial views over the Great Blue Hole and boat rides along the barrier reef. Inland forest roads are dry and easy to navigate.
Increasing clouds and rain showers begin to obscure aerial views of the reef. The inland forests turn lush and green, though some unpaved routes become muddy.

Heavy rains and frequent storms churn up coastal waters, reducing the striking color contrasts of the marine sinkholes. Low cloud cover often blocks scenic flights, and dirt roads into the forest reserves flood.
Rains begin to taper off, slowly restoring water clarity around the cayes. Aerial flights over the reef resume more regular schedules as the heavy cloud cover breaks.

gemini.depth_why: Access to the high-elevation rim and scenic byways changes distinctly with the heavy winter snowpack and summer melting.
gemini.overview: The deep blue caldera of Crater Lake and the volcanic peaks of the Cascades define the scenery of this region. Visitors can drive through ancient lava fields, pine forests, and river canyons around Bend. The high-elevation viewpoints and rim roads are fully accessible only during the short summer season.

blurbs.text: Heavy snow closes the North Entrance and Rim Drive at Crater Lake, as well as the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway. Views of the caldera are limited to the South Entrance, and winter storms frequently obscure the mountains.
Plowing begins on the high-elevation roads, but the Rim Drive and Cascade Lakes routes remain closed by deep snowpack. Lower-elevation lava fields and river canyons around Bend are clear.

The snowpack recedes enough for the North Entrance and parts of the Rim Drive to open. High-elevation trails may still hold snow, but the main viewpoints over the caldera and the Cascade peaks are accessible.
The full Rim Drive around Crater Lake and the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway are open. Visitors can drive to high viewpoints and hike the volcanic trails without snow blocking the paths.
Early snows begin to dust the Cascade peaks. The main scenic drives usually remain open through the first half of the month, though sudden storms can close high-elevation roads temporarily.

gemini.depth_why: The urban views and river embankments do not change with the seasons.
gemini.overview: The Brandenburg Gate and the embankments of the Spree River provide the signature views of the German capital. The wide riverways and extensive city parks create pleasant, modest vistas across the flat urban terrain.

blurbs.text: The broad avenues leading to the Brandenburg Gate and the paved paths along the Spree River provide the most recognizable vantage points. The city's flat terrain keeps the focus entirely on its urban layout, wide waterways, and the forested edges of the Tiergarten.

gemini.depth_why: Scores drop during the summer monsoon when clouds obscure the mountains, and peak in spring and autumn.
gemini.overview: Bhutan is defined by the Himalayas, with deep valleys, dense forests and high passes. The signature view is the Tiger's Nest monastery clinging to a cliffside, while the Punakha Dzong sits at the confluence of two rivers. The scenery is best seen in spring and autumn, when the skies are clear and the mountain views are unobstructed.

blurbs.text: Winter brings clear skies and sharp views of the high peaks, though snow can close the higher passes like Dochula. The valleys are cold but accessible.
Spring is a prime time for mountain views before the monsoon arrives. The valleys are green, and the high passes are clear of winter snow.
The summer monsoon brings heavy rain and low clouds that often hide the high peaks. Landslides can occasionally block mountain roads.
The monsoon rains begin to ease, and the clouds start to lift, revealing the mountains again. The forests and valleys are lush from the summer rain.
Autumn offers the clearest skies of the year, with sharp, unobstructed views of the Himalayas. The weather is dry, making it the best time for the high passes and viewpoints.
Early winter keeps the skies clear for mountain viewing, though temperatures drop and snow begins to accumulate on the highest routes.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery and access to it remain consistent throughout the year.
gemini.overview: The Big Island is defined by its active geology, with the active caldera of Kilauea and the high summit of Mauna Kea dominating the interior. The coasts range from the dry, lava-strewn Kona and Kohala sides to the lush Hamakua coast, known for deep valleys and tall waterfalls. The landscape shifts rapidly from barren volcanic rock to dense tropical forest.

blurbs.text: The volcanic landscapes of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park and the high-altitude views from Mauna Kea are accessible. The Hamakua coast offers views of Akaka Falls and Waipio Valley, while the western coasts show stark contrasts between black lava fields and the ocean.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise in spring, peak in summer, and fall in autumn and winter as snow and cold limit access.
gemini.overview: The Black Forest is known for its dense, dark evergreen woods, rolling hills, and deep valleys. The scenery is defined by wooded ridges, half-timbered villages, and the multi-tiered Triberg waterfalls. The best views are found along the Schwarzwaldhochstraße (Black Forest High Road), which offers sweeping panoramas over the Rhine plain.

blurbs.text: Snow covers the higher elevations, transforming the dark woods into a winter landscape. Some minor roads and trails may be difficult to navigate, but the main routes remain clear. The Triberg waterfalls often freeze into ice formations.
Snow melts from the valleys and lower hills, though patches remain on the highest ridges. The forests begin to green, and the waterfalls flow heavily with the spring runoff.

The forests are dense and green, and the weather is warm enough for long drives and walks. The Schwarzwaldhochstraße offers clear views over the valleys and the Rhine plain, and the trails around the Triberg waterfalls are fully accessible.

Autumn brings color to the deciduous trees mixed among the evergreens, creating a contrast against the dark pines. The air is crisp, and visibility from the high roads is often excellent before the winter snows begin.

gemini.depth_why: The vineyards change from bare winter branches to full summer green and autumn colors.
gemini.overview: The primary views are the flat, elegant urban riverfront and the surrounding vine-covered estates of the Médoc. The Place de la Bourse reflects in a massive water mirror, creating a striking symmetrical view of the 18th-century facades. Beyond the city limits, the landscape transitions into orderly rows of vineyards stretching across gentle slopes.

blurbs.text: The vines are bare and pruned back for the winter, leaving the vineyard slopes stark and quiet. The city's riverfront architecture remains the primary visual draw, though the water mirror is often drained or less reflective during colder stretches.

The vineyards of the Médoc fill in with green foliage, eventually turning gold and red by early autumn. The water mirror at the Place de la Bourse is active, reflecting the grand architecture along the Garonne river.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise and fall with the monsoon rains, which affect visibility and access to the rainforests and mountains.
gemini.overview: Malaysian Borneo is defined by its ancient rainforests and the granite peaks of Mount Kinabalu. The primary draws are the dense, towering canopy of the Danum Valley and the winding Kinabatangan River, where boat trips reveal the jungle banks. The scenery is best viewed during the drier months, when trails are clear and the mountain is visible.

blurbs.text: Heavy monsoon rains often obscure the views and swell the rivers. Trails in the rainforests can be muddy and difficult to navigate, and the peaks of Mount Kinabalu are frequently hidden by thick clouds.
The rains begin to ease, and the rivers slowly recede. The rainforest canopy becomes easier to explore, and the mountain views start to clear as the heavy cloud cover lifts.

The drier weather brings the clearest views of Mount Kinabalu's granite summit. The trails through the Danum Valley are at their most accessible, and boat trips along the Kinabatangan River offer unobstructed views of the dense jungle banks.
Rain showers become more frequent as the wet season approaches. The rainforest remains lush and green, though low clouds may begin to gather around the higher elevations.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise as the floodwaters arrive and peak in the dry winter months, then fall as the waters recede and the rains return.
gemini.overview: The Okavango Delta is an inland river system that spills into the Kalahari Desert, creating a vast network of channels, lagoons, and islands. The scenery is defined by the water itself, best seen from a traditional mokoro canoe gliding through the reeds, or from a small plane above the floodplains. The landscape changes with the annual flood, which peaks during the dry winter months.

blurbs.text: The summer rains bring thick vegetation, but the main floodwaters have not yet arrived. Water levels in the channels are lower, and some areas may be less accessible by boat, though the landscape is green and lush.
The rains end and the annual floodwaters begin to arrive from the Angolan highlands. The channels slowly fill, expanding the waterways and transforming the dry plains into a flooded landscape.

The floodwaters reach their highest levels, creating the classic delta scenery of deep channels, lily-covered lagoons, and flooded plains. This is the prime time to explore the waterways by mokoro or boat, with clear skies and dry weather.
The floodwaters recede and the landscape dries out, shrinking the channels and lagoons. The summer rains begin late in the year, bringing new growth to the plains.

gemini.depth_why: Visibility and daylight hours change with the seasons, affecting the views from the hills.
gemini.overview: Budapest's scenery is defined by the wide Danube River dividing the flat Pest side from the steep Buda Hills. The signature view looks across the water to the Parliament building and the Chain Bridge. Viewpoints like Gellért Hill and the Fisherman's Bastion provide sweeping panoramas of the river basin.

blurbs.text: Winter brings early sunsets and occasional fog that can obscure the river basin from higher vantage points.
Spring clears the winter haze, improving visibility from the Buda Hills across the river.
Long daylight hours provide ample time to walk the riverbanks and take in the panoramas from Gellért Hill.
Autumn brings clear skies and changing colors to the trees lining the Danube and the slopes of Buda.

gemini.na_reason: Flat urban setting; city beauty belongs to Architecture.
gemini.depth_why: Not applicable.
The scenery is accessible and visible year-round with no significant seasonal changes.
gemini.overview: The Canary Islands are defined by dramatic volcanic landscapes, from the towering peak of Mount Teide to the shifting sand dunes of Fuerteventura. Visitors can drive through the ancient laurel forests of the Anaga mountains or hike among the striking rock formations of the Roques de García. The rugged coastlines offer steep cliffs and black sand beaches, providing diverse scenery across the archipelago.

blurbs.text: The volcanic peaks, coastal cliffs and ancient forests are fully accessible. Clear days offer expansive views from Mount Teide and the Anaga mountains, while the dunes of Fuerteventura remain a striking contrast to the ocean.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise and fall with the seasons, reflecting the appeal of the coastal scenery in warmer months versus the starker, colder winter.
gemini.overview: The draw here is the classic New England coastline, defined by long sandy beaches, dunes, and historic maritime villages. The scenery is flat but striking, especially the sweeping dunes around Provincetown and the gray-shingled towns of Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard. The views are best in the warmer months when the coastal light is bright and the ferries run frequently.

blurbs.text: Winter brings a stark, quiet beauty to the coast. The beaches and dunes are empty, and the gray-shingled villages look especially austere against the winter sky, though cold winds make long walks less appealing.
Spring slowly warms the coast. The dunes and beaches remain quiet, offering peaceful views of the shoreline before the summer crowds arrive, though the water and wind are still chilly.

Early summer brings bright coastal light and warming weather. The dunes around Provincetown and the island villages are vibrant, and ferry access to Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard is fully operational.

The coastal scenery is at its most classic. The long sandy beaches, sweeping dunes, and historic maritime villages are bathed in summer sun, making for ideal conditions to explore the shoreline and the islands.
Autumn brings crisp air and a return to quieter coastal views. The beaches empty out, and the dunes take on a softer light, offering peaceful scenery as the busy season winds down.

gemini.depth_why: Visibility and access change with the dry summer and wet winter seasons.
gemini.overview: The dramatic meeting of steep sandstone mountains and the Atlantic Ocean defines the scenery of the Cape Peninsula. Table Mountain rises directly above the city bowl, offering views of the coastline and surrounding peaks from its flat summit. Farther south, the cliffs of Cape Point drop into the sea. Chapman's Peak Drive cuts into the coastal mountainside for miles of ocean views.

blurbs.text: Dry, clear days offer the best visibility from the peaks and coastal roads. Strong southeasterly winds occasionally push a thick layer of cloud over Table Mountain, which can obscure the summit and halt the cableway.

The strong summer winds die down, leaving calmer air for coastal drives. Rain showers and low clouds begin to appear more frequently as autumn progresses, occasionally blocking the views from higher elevations.

Winter storms bring heavy rain and thick fog that frequently hide the mountains and coastline. Clear days between the fronts offer sharp views, but the cableway and mountain trails often close in poor weather.
The winter rains taper off and the skies clear, restoring long sightlines down the peninsula. Lingering cold fronts can still bring sudden cloud cover to the peaks.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with snow cover, trail access, and glacier visibility across the seasons.
gemini.overview: The Mont Blanc massif dominates the Chamonix valley, offering some of the most dramatic alpine scenery in the world. The Aiguille du Midi cable car provides a close-up view of the peaks and the Mer de Glace glacier. Summer opens the high hiking trails and mountain passes, while winter covers the landscape in deep snow for skiing and snowshoeing.

blurbs.text: Deep snow covers the valley and the peaks. The Aiguille du Midi cable car runs, offering clear, freezing views of the Mont Blanc massif, though high hiking trails and some mountain passes are closed for the winter.
Snow begins to melt in the valley, but the high peaks remain white. Trails at lower elevations start to clear, though high-altitude routes and passes are still blocked by snow.

The high alpine trails are clear of snow, opening up the full range of viewpoints across the Mont Blanc massif. The Mer de Glace is accessible, and the long days allow for extensive drives and walks through the valleys and over the passes.

Autumn brings changing colors to the lower forests. The high peaks may see early dustings of snow, and while some high trails begin to close, the main viewpoints like the Aiguille du Midi remain accessible.

The transition to winter brings early snows and shorter days. Many high trails are closed, and the landscape is caught between autumn bareness and winter snow cover, though the main peaks are still visible.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery changes with the agricultural cycle of the vineyards, from bare winter branches to lush summer green and golden autumn foliage.
gemini.overview: The region's visual appeal centers on its rolling, vine-covered hillsides that stretch across the Marne valley and the Montagne de Reims. Historic villages and the distant spires of the Reims Cathedral provide a classic rural French backdrop to the agricultural landscape. The scenery peaks during the autumn harvest when the vineyards turn vibrant shades of gold and red.

blurbs.text: Winter leaves the vineyards bare and the hillsides stark, with frequent gray skies and occasional frost covering the fields.
Spring brings bud break to the vines, adding faint green hues to the rolling hills and valleys.
The vineyards fill out into lush, dense green canopies that blanket the slopes of the Montagne de Reims.
The autumn harvest transforms the landscape as the vine leaves turn brilliant shades of yellow, gold, and deep red.
The bright autumn foliage drops quickly, leaving the hillsides mostly bare as the first winter chills set in.

gemini.depth_why: The landscape is visible year-round, with marsh grasses changing from green to brown in the winter.
gemini.overview: The coastal Lowcountry is defined by flat, tidal salt marshes and maritime forests of live oaks draped in Spanish moss. The urban centers feature historic waterfronts, such as Charleston's pastel Rainbow Row, and Savannah's shaded, park-like squares. The views are subtle and low-lying, best seen from coastal drives or by walking the historic districts.

blurbs.text: The tidal marsh grasses turn a golden brown. The evergreen live oaks and their Spanish moss keep the maritime forests and city squares shaded, though deciduous trees lose their leaves.
The salt marshes are bright green and the maritime forests are dense. The evergreen live oaks provide heavy shade over the city squares and coastal roads.

gemini.depth_why: Visibility changes drastically with the dry season smoke and the monsoon rains.
gemini.overview: The forested mountains and river valleys of Northern Thailand provide a lush backdrop to the region's ancient temples and rural villages. The peaks of Doi Inthanon offer sweeping views over the surrounding highlands, while dense jungles hide tiered waterfalls and winding mountain passes. The clearest views come in the cooler, dry months before the agricultural burning season begins.

blurbs.text: Clear skies reveal the full depth of the mountain ranges and valleys. The air is cool, making drives up to Doi Inthanon and walks to the region's waterfalls comfortable, with sharp visibility across the forested highlands.
Haze begins to build in the valleys as the dry weather continues. The mountain outlines soften, though the higher viewpoints still offer sweeping sights over the jungle canopy.

Heavy smoke from agricultural burning fills the air, severely reducing visibility. The mountain views are largely obscured by a thick haze, and the scenery is mostly limited to the immediate surroundings.
The first rains begin to clear the lingering smoke from the air. Visibility improves, though low clouds often hang over the peaks and the waterfalls are just starting to regain their flow.

Frequent monsoon rains turn the forests a deep, vibrant green and fill the rivers and waterfalls to their peaks. Heavy cloud cover often hides the highest viewpoints, and some unpaved rural roads become difficult to navigate.
The rains taper off, leaving the jungles lush and the waterfalls flowing heavily. The skies clear, bringing back sharp views of the mountain ridges and valleys.

gemini.depth_why: The dry and wet seasons dictate water clarity and visibility, creating distinct periods for viewing the landscapes.
gemini.overview: Chiapas is defined by its dense forests, deep canyons, and a network of rivers and waterfalls. The Cañón del Sumidero cuts through the terrain with vertical walls rising thousands of feet above the water. The cascades of Agua Azul flow in wide tiers through the jungle. The colonial architecture of San Cristóbal de las Casas sits in a highland valley, providing a built backdrop to the natural environment.

blurbs.text: The dry season keeps the rivers and waterfalls running clear, showing off the bright turquoise color at Agua Azul. Forest trails are mostly dry, and the canyon viewpoints offer clear lines of sight.
The first rains begin to swell the rivers, increasing the flow over the cascades. The water color starts to shift from blue to green as runoff enters the streams.
Heavy summer rains turn the rivers and waterfalls muddy and brown, hiding the famous blue tones. Low clouds and fog frequently settle into the highland valleys and obscure the canyon rims.
The rains taper off and the rivers begin to settle. The water slowly clears, returning to its lighter shades, and the forests are thick and green from the wet season.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with the distinct seasons, from clear summer access to wet, cloudy winters.
gemini.overview: The Chilean Lake District is defined by the snow-capped cones of the Osorno and Villarrica volcanoes rising directly above deep, glacially carved lakes. Ancient lenga and araucaria forests cover the lower slopes, cut by fast-flowing rivers and waterfalls. The clearest views and most accessible trails run from late spring through early autumn.

blurbs.text: Summer brings the clearest skies for viewing the Osorno and Villarrica volcanoes. High-elevation trails in Huerquehue National Park are free of snow, allowing hikers to reach the alpine lakes and ancient araucaria and lenga forests.

The lenga forests turn deep red and orange, contrasting with the evergreen araucaria trees and the blue lakes. Clouds begin to gather more frequently around the volcano peaks, and rain showers increase.

Heavy autumn rains set in, and low clouds often obscure the volcanoes. Lower-elevation walks to waterfalls like Petrohué remain accessible, though higher trails become muddy and see their first snows.

Winter brings heavy rain to the valleys and deep snow to the mountains. Many trails in the national parks close, and persistent cloud cover hides the signature volcano views, though the snow-covered peaks look dramatic on rare clear days.

Spring snowmelt swells the rivers, making the Petrohué Waterfalls and other cascades particularly powerful. Rain and fog are still common, but the lower valleys turn bright green as the weather slowly warms.
The snow line retreats up the volcanoes, opening up more hiking routes through the forests. Skies clear more often, revealing the classic views of the peaks mirrored in the lakes below.

gemini.depth_why: The landscape changes distinctly from frozen winter ice to summer open water and exposed tundra.
gemini.overview: Churchill sits at the edge of the subarctic tundra and the rocky shores of Hudson Bay. The landscape transitions from a vast, frozen expanse of sea ice in the winter to exposed rock and low-lying vegetation along the Churchill River estuary in the summer.

blurbs.text: The tundra and Hudson Bay are locked in thick ice and snow, creating a vast, white subarctic expanse.
The ice on the bay begins to fracture and melt, exposing the rocky coastline and muddy plains.
The bay is open water, and the flat tundra reveals its rocky surface and low-lying vegetation along the Churchill River estuary.
Ice forms along the edges of Hudson Bay, gradually expanding to cover the water as snow returns to the flat plains.

gemini.depth_why: Scores follow the dry and wet seasons of the Andes.
gemini.overview: The Colombian Andes are known for steep, green mountainsides and the high-altitude cloud forests that cover them. The signature view is the Cocora Valley, where the world's tallest wax palms rise from misty pastures. The coffee region adds rolling hills dotted with traditional villages, while higher elevations hold paramo ecosystems and scattered glaciers.

blurbs.text: The first dry season brings the clearest skies to the mountains. The trails through the Cocora Valley and the high paramo are mostly dry, making it easier to reach viewpoints and see the wax palms against blue skies.

The first wet season brings frequent rain and heavy cloud cover to the mountains. The cloud forests live up to their name, often shrouded in mist that obscures the longer views across the valleys, and trails can become deeply muddy.
A second dry season clears the air again. The green hills of the coffee region and the high peaks are visible, and the dirt roads connecting the mountain villages are easier to navigate.

The second wet season is typically the rainiest time in the Andes. Low clouds and fog frequently block the views of the peaks and valleys, and heavy rains can cause landslides that temporarily close mountain roads.
The rains begin to taper off as the year ends. The valleys are lush and green from the wet season, and the clouds start to lift, revealing more of the mountain scenery.

gemini.depth_why: The year divides into a clear dry season with optimal coastal views and a wetter season with reduced visibility.
gemini.overview: The Colombian Caribbean pairs tropical coastal scenery with the striking colonial architecture of Cartagena's walled old town. Visitors take boats out to the Rosario Islands to see coral reefs and white-sand beaches set against clear blue water. Inland, the landscape shifts to dense mangroves and coastal forests.

blurbs.text: Clear skies and calm waters make this the best time to view the coastal scenery and take boat trips out to the islands.
Passing rain showers become more frequent, occasionally clouding the water and softening the coastal views, though mornings often remain clear.
Heavy rains and overcast skies can obscure the horizon and disrupt boat access to the offshore islands.

gemini.depth_why: The flat coastal and canal scenery remains consistent across the seasons.
gemini.overview: Copenhagen is built on flat coastal islands, and its most recognizable views are defined by water. The signature sight is Nyhavn, a harbor lined with brightly painted townhouses and wooden boats. Beyond the canals, the surrounding terrain is mostly flat, offering modest coastal stretches and quiet harbor walks rather than dramatic natural features.

blurbs.text: The flat coastal setting means the most notable sights are found along the water, particularly the historic canals and the harbor front.

gemini.depth_why: The scores rise through spring to a summer peak and fall through autumn, driven by daylight and weather on the coast path.
gemini.overview: Cornwall is defined by its rugged coastline, where high cliffs drop into the Atlantic and sandy coves sit between rocky headlands. The South West Coast Path traces the entire edge, passing landmarks like Land's End and the tidal island of St Michael's Mount. Inland, the scenery shifts to rolling farmland and quiet villages, but the coast remains the main draw. The views are clearest and easiest to reach from late spring through summer.

blurbs.text: Winter brings short days, frequent rain and strong winds off the Atlantic. The coast path is often muddy and exposed, and low light limits the views of the cliffs and coves. St Michael's Mount and the headlands look dramatic in rough weather, but access is harder.

Spring lengthens the days and dries out the trails. The coast path becomes easier to walk, and the views of the cliffs and the sea open up as the weather settles. The headlands and coves are quiet before the summer crowds arrive.

Long days and warmer weather make this the best time to see the coast. The South West Coast Path is fully accessible, offering clear views of Land's End, St Ives harbor and the rocky shoreline. The sea and sky are at their brightest, though the main viewpoints get busy.

Autumn brings shorter days and a return to wetter, windier weather. The coast path remains open, but the views are often softened by mist or rain. The crowds thin out, leaving the cliffs and beaches quieter.

gemini.depth_why: Scores drop during the wet season when clouds and rain obscure views and make trails muddy.
gemini.overview: Costa Rica is known for its dense cloud forests, active volcanoes, and tropical coastlines. The signature views are the perfect cone of Arenal Volcano rising above the jungle and the beaches of Manuel Antonio National Park meeting the rainforest. Rivers and waterfalls cut through the interior, while the coasts offer long stretches of sand and rocky coves.

blurbs.text: The dry season brings clear skies, making this the best time to see the peak of Arenal Volcano and the sweeping coastal views at Manuel Antonio. Trails through the cloud forests and down to waterfalls are mostly dry and accessible.
The transition to the wet season begins. Clouds start to gather around the volcanic peaks and afternoon showers become common, but mornings usually offer clear views of the coasts and forests.
Rain is frequent, swelling the rivers and waterfalls to their most powerful flows. The forests are lush and green, though low clouds often hide the higher mountain peaks and volcanoes.

Heavy rains define the peak of the wet season. Trails can be muddy or washed out, and thick clouds frequently obscure the volcanoes and coastal viewpoints. Waterfalls are dramatic, but reaching them can be difficult.

The rains begin to ease, and the landscapes are exceptionally green from the wet season. Cloud cover starts to lift, revealing the mountains and volcanoes more often, though trails may still be muddy.
The dry season returns, clearing the skies and drying out the trails. The forests remain lush from the recent rains, and views of the coastlines and volcanic peaks are consistently clear.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise slightly in the warmer, greener months and fall in the colder, barer winter.
gemini.overview: The Cotswolds are defined by their rolling hills, quiet woodlands, and the honey-colored stone of their historic villages. The landscape is gentle and rural, with narrow lanes connecting small settlements set against green pastures and low ridges. The most famous views are the villages themselves, such as Bibury and Castle Combe, which blend seamlessly into the surrounding countryside.

blurbs.text: The hills and woodlands are bare, and the landscape takes on a muted, quiet tone. The stone villages stand out sharply against the winter fields, though short days limit the time for walking the rural lanes.
Spring brings new green to the pastures and woodlands. The rolling hills begin to brighten, and the longer days make it easier to explore the viewpoints and village settings.
The rural scenery is at its greenest and most vibrant. The gentle hills, woodlands, and pastures are fully leafed out, providing a lush backdrop for the honey-stone villages.
The green pastures begin to fade, and the woodlands take on autumn colors. The changing foliage adds warmth to the landscape around the stone villages before the trees lose their leaves.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise from winter lows to a summer peak as access to islands and coastal viewpoints improves.
gemini.overview: The Dalmatian Coast is defined by its dramatic meeting of mountains and the Adriatic Sea, with steep limestone cliffs dropping into clear water. The signature views are the walled city of Dubrovnik rising directly from the coast and the terraced waterfalls of Krka and Plitvice Lakes inland. Hundreds of islands dot the coastline, offering quiet coves and pine-forested shores.

blurbs.text: Winter brings quiet to the coast, with rougher seas and fewer ferries running to the islands. The coastal mountains and walled cities remain striking, though inland waterfalls like Plitvice may be partially frozen or surrounded by snow, and some trails close for safety.

Spring brings rising water levels to the inland rivers, making the waterfalls at Krka and Plitvice particularly powerful. Coastal drives offer clear views of the islands, and ferry schedules begin to expand as the weather warms.

The coastal scenery is at its best, with calm, clear waters highlighting the limestone cliffs and island archipelagos. Full ferry schedules allow easy access to remote island viewpoints, and the long days provide ample time for coastal drives and walking the walls of Dubrovnik.

Autumn colors begin to appear in the forests around the inland lakes and waterfalls. The coastal views remain clear, though ferry services to the smaller islands start to reduce as the season winds down.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery itself does not change through the year, and access remains open.
gemini.overview: Death Valley is one of the world's premier desert landscapes, defined by vast salt flats, painted canyons, and towering dunes. The scenery is stark and expansive, with viewpoints looking out over the lowest point in North America. The views remain unchanged across the seasons.

blurbs.text: The desert scenery is fully visible. Badwater Basin offers a vast expanse of white salt flats, while Zabriskie Point looks over deeply eroded, colorful badlands. The Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes provide classic, rippled desert views.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise as the park road opens and snow clears, peaking in summer, then fall as winter closes access.
gemini.overview: The Alaska Range dominates the Interior, anchored by Denali, the highest peak in North America. Visitors come for the vast tundra, braided rivers, and glaciers that shape the valleys. The signature view is Denali itself, often seen from Wonder Lake or on a flightseeing trip, though the mountain creates its own weather and is frequently hidden by clouds.

blurbs.text: Deep snow and extreme cold limit access to the Interior. The Denali Park Road is mostly closed to vehicles, and daylight is brief, leaving only a few hours to see the snow-covered peaks.

Days lengthen significantly, bringing more light to the snow-covered Alaska Range. The park road remains closed to most traffic, but flightseeing offers views of the glaciers and peaks before the spring thaw begins.
The snow begins to melt, and the lower sections of the Denali Park Road open to vehicles. The tundra is still brown, but the rivers start to flow freely as the ice breaks up.

The park road is open as far as conditions allow, providing access to the deep Interior and viewpoints like Wonder Lake. The tundra is green, and long daylight hours give ample time to watch for the clouds to part around Denali.

The tundra turns bright red and gold, creating a striking contrast against the first dustings of new snow on the peaks. The park road begins to close as the month progresses and winter weather returns.
Snow covers the landscape again, and the park road closes to most vehicles. The views are stark and white, with shortening days limiting the time to see the mountains.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise from winter lows to a peak in the autumn harvest season.
gemini.overview: The Douro Valley is defined by its steep, terraced vineyards rising directly from the Douro River. The scenery is best seen from the water or the winding roads that trace the valley walls. Porto anchors the region with its own riverfront views, where the city's historic center steps down to the water.

blurbs.text: Winter brings bare vines and cooler, often damp weather. The river and the terraced hills remain visible, but the landscape lacks the color of the growing season.
Spring brings green growth back to the terraced vineyards. The weather warms, making boat trips on the river and drives along the valley roads more comfortable.
The vines are fully green and the valley is warm and bright. The steep terraces stand out clearly against the river, and viewpoints along the winding roads offer long sights down the valley.
Autumn turns the terraced vineyards red, gold, and yellow. The colors stand out sharply against the river and the steep valley walls, making this the most striking time to see the landscape.
The autumn color fades and the vines go bare as winter approaches. The valley is quieter, and the views rely on the shape of the terraces and the river itself.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery itself (desert dunes and the city skyline) does not change with the seasons.
gemini.overview: Dubai is known for the sharp contrast between its futuristic skyline and the surrounding desert. The signature view is the Burj Khalifa and the dense cluster of skyscrapers rising from the flat coastal plain. Beyond the city limits, the landscape shifts immediately to rolling sand dunes, which can be seen on drives into the desert.

blurbs.text: The views of the city skyline and the surrounding desert dunes remain constant. Visibility is generally clear, though occasional dust storms can obscure the horizon.

gemini.depth_why: The year divides into a clear dry season, a wet season, and a transitional period with a short dry spell.
gemini.overview: The Ecuadorian Andes are defined by the Avenue of the Volcanoes, a high-altitude corridor of glaciated peaks and deep valleys. The terrain shifts from the perfect cone of Cotopaxi and the massive slopes of Chimborazo to the steep, water-filled caldera of Quilotoa. The region also features high paramo grasslands and lower cloud forests draped over the western and eastern slopes.

blurbs.text: The dry season brings the clearest skies to the highlands, revealing the snow-capped summits of Cotopaxi and Chimborazo. High winds sweep across the paramo, but the lack of heavy rain keeps the trails to the Quilotoa crater and the high mountain passes firmly packed.

Clouds begin to gather around the high peaks, and afternoon rain showers become more frequent across the valleys. A short dry spell often arrives around the turn of the year, opening up brief windows of clear morning visibility for the major volcanoes.

Heavy cloud cover frequently obscures the highest glaciated peaks, and persistent rain softens the trails and rural dirt roads. The lower cloud forests and paramo grasslands turn deep green, though visitors must rely on early mornings for a chance to see the volcanic cones.

gemini.depth_why: Scores dip in winter due to short daylight and frequent low clouds obscuring the views.
gemini.overview: Edinburgh's dramatic topography is built across a series of extinct volcanoes and rocky crags. The primary natural draws are Arthur's Seat and the Salisbury Crags, which rise sharply above the streets and offer sweeping views of the skyline and the distant Firth of Forth. The Castle Rock provides another striking vantage point, anchoring the city's rugged profile.

blurbs.text: Short daylight hours and frequent low clouds or fog can obscure the wider views from the summits, and winter weather often makes the steep paths up the crags slippery.
Long daylight hours allow for late evening walks up Arthur's Seat and the Salisbury Crags, with clear views over the city and the water.

gemini.depth_why: The desert, river, and coastal landscapes remain visible and accessible without seasonal closures.
gemini.overview: The region is defined by the stark contrast between the Sahara's arid expanses and the lush, palm-lined banks of the Nile. Visitors look for the silhouettes of the Giza pyramids against the desert sky and the rugged mountains meeting the Red Sea coast. The scenery relies on vast dunes, ancient river valleys, and clear coastal waters.

blurbs.text: The desert skies are generally clear, offering unobstructed views of the Nile Valley and the Red Sea coastline. Spring winds occasionally lift dust that softens the horizon, but the stark dunes, riverbanks, and ancient monuments remain prominent.

gemini.depth_why: Scores form clear seasonal stages based on snow cover, trail access, and daylight.
gemini.overview: The region is defined by the sheer granite spires of Mount Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre rising sharply above the Patagonian steppe. Massive ice fields feed into the surrounding lakes, most notably the towering blue wall of the Perito Moreno Glacier. The valleys hold dense lenga forests and glacial rivers that are best viewed during the long days of the austral summer.

blurbs.text: Long daylight hours keep the mountain trails and glacier viewpoints fully accessible. The granite peaks are mostly clear of winter snow, and the ice fields are highly active.
Autumn brings red and orange foliage to the lenga forests below the peaks. Daylight wanes, but the main viewpoints and valleys remain easy to reach.
Snow begins to accumulate on higher trails, limiting access to some mountain viewpoints as the transition to winter accelerates.
Short winter days and deep snow close many high-elevation paths. The main glacier walkways remain open, offering views of the ice against a snow-covered landscape.
Melting snow gradually reopens the higher trekking routes. The ice fields and mountain bases become easier to reach as the days lengthen.

gemini.depth_why: Scores drop during the rainy season when roads and trails become difficult.
gemini.overview: Ethiopia is defined by its dramatic highlands, deep valleys, and ancient rock-hewn settlements. The Simien Mountains offer sheer cliffs and deep gorges, while the Danakil Depression provides a stark, volcanic desert landscape. The rock churches of Lalibela blend human history with the rugged terrain. The best views are found during the dry season when skies are clear and remote roads are passable.

blurbs.text: Clear skies and dry trails make this the best time to see the Simien Mountains and the Danakil Depression. The landscapes are vivid, and remote routes are fully passable.
The short rains begin, bringing some clouds and occasional showers. The highlands turn greener, though some dirt roads may become muddy and visibility can occasionally drop.
Heavy rains dominate the highlands. Cloud cover often obscures the mountain views, and many unpaved roads and trails in the Simien Mountains become difficult or impassable.
The heavy rains taper off, leaving the highlands lush and green. Waterfalls are at their peak flow, though some roads may still be recovering from the wet season.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery changes with the distinct wet and dry seasons, which alter water levels, reflections, and trail access.
gemini.overview: The Everglades is defined by its vast, flat expanses of sawgrass prairies and dense mangrove forests. Visitors view these wetland landscapes from raised boardwalks, kayaks navigating coastal waterways, and airboats crossing the shallow marshes. The scenery is clearest and most accessible during the dry winter months.

blurbs.text: The dry season lowers water levels, exposing textured mudflats and making the sawgrass prairies stand out against the sky. Clear skies make this the best time to paddle the mangrove tunnels or walk the raised boardwalks.
Early rains begin to fill the marshes, altering the reflections in the shallow waters. Rising humidity and afternoon clouds start to obscure distant views across the prairies.

The wet season floods the prairies, turning the landscape into a vast, unbroken sheet of water. Heavy afternoon thunderstorms frequently block visibility and limit access to open-water kayaking and exposed trails.
The heavy summer rains taper off, leaving the wetlands fully inundated and green. Receding storm clouds open up wider views of the flooded sawgrass plains before the dry season takes hold.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with the austral seasons, dropping in winter due to short daylight and harder access to remote areas.
gemini.overview: The Falkland Islands are defined by rugged, windswept coasts and the vast, treeless expanses known as the Camp. White sand beaches contrast with dark Atlantic waters, forming the iconic coastal views of the archipelago. The best viewing conditions align with the long daylight hours of the austral summer.

blurbs.text: Long daylight hours illuminate the white sand beaches and rolling, treeless plains of the Camp. The coastal views are at their clearest, making it the best time to explore the rugged shorelines.
Autumn brings shorter days and cooler winds across the open landscapes. The rugged coastlines remain striking, though skies are often grayer and the light fades earlier.
Winter means very short days and frequent frost or snow, which can obscure the coastal tracks and limit access to remote viewpoints across the open land.
Spring thaws the ground, and lengthening days slowly reveal the stark beauty of the coastal cliffs and open plains once again.

gemini.depth_why: Access to the cliffs and outer islands changes with the daylight and ferry schedules.
gemini.overview: The Faroe Islands are defined by sheer basalt cliffs dropping into the North Atlantic and steep, treeless mountains. The signature view is Múlafossur waterfall plunging directly into the ocean below the village of Gásadalur. Visitors drive narrow coastal roads and hike to viewpoints like the summit of Slættaratindur or the sea cliffs of Mykines.

blurbs.text: Short daylight hours limit time on the trails, and winter storms frequently obscure the mountains. The coastal roads remain open, but high winds often make cliff viewpoints difficult to reach.
Daylight lengthens rapidly, revealing the snow-dusted peaks of Slættaratindur. Trails are often muddy and some remote mountain passes remain blocked by lingering snow.
Ferries resume service to Mykines, opening access to its dramatic sea cliffs. The valleys turn green, and the waterfalls flow heavily from the spring melt.

Long summer days provide nearly endless light for driving the coastal routes and hiking to Múlafossur. The sea is calmest, allowing reliable ferry access to the outer islands and clear views from the highest summits.
Autumn brings low light that casts long shadows across the basalt cliffs. Ferries to the outer islands reduce their schedules, and low clouds begin to settle more frequently over the mountain passes.

gemini.depth_why: Scores form clear groups based on the transition between the wet and dry seasons.
gemini.overview: Fiji is defined by its coastal scenery of turquoise lagoons and white-sand islands. The Mamanuca and Yasawa island chains provide classic South Pacific views of palm-fringed beaches and shallow reefs visible through clear water. Inland, the larger islands like Viti Levu feature modest volcanic mountains and dense tropical forests.

blurbs.text: Heavy rains and frequent cloud cover dull the bright colors of the lagoons. Storms often churn up the water, reducing clarity for coastal views, though the inland forests grow thick and green.
The heavy rains begin to ease, and the skies clear more often. The turquoise waters regain their bright hues as the sediment settles, making the island views much sharper.

Clear skies and dry air create the best conditions for taking in the coastal scenery. The contrast between the white sand, deep blue ocean, and bright lagoons is at its sharpest, and visibility across the water is excellent.
Cloud cover gradually increases as the dry season ends. The lagoons remain bright and striking, but occasional showers begin to soften the distant views of the volcanic peaks.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery of the Galápagos Islands is volcanic and coastal, remaining visible and accessible throughout the year.
gemini.overview: The Galápagos Islands are defined by stark volcanic coasts and dramatic rock formations rising from the Pacific. The signature view is Pinnacle Rock on Bartolomé Island, a jagged volcanic cone flanked by beaches. Beyond the famous sights, the archipelago offers quiet bays, lava fields, and rugged shorelines that remain unchanged across the seasons.

blurbs.text: The volcanic landscapes and coastal formations are visible and accessible. The stark contrast between the dark lava fields, white sand beaches, and the ocean provides the primary scenery, with Pinnacle Rock standing as the most recognizable landmark.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise in the dry season when visibility is best and fall slightly in the wet season.
gemini.overview: The Great Barrier Reef is one of the world's premier coastal landscapes, defined by its vast network of coral cays, turquoise waters, and white sand beaches. The signature views are seen from the water or the air, where the scale of the reef systems becomes clear. Whitehaven Beach is a major draw for its swirling silica sands and clear shallows. The scenery is best viewed during the dry season, when the water is clearest and the skies are mostly sunny.

blurbs.text: The wet season brings heavy rains, higher humidity, and occasional cyclones. Cloud cover and runoff can reduce water clarity, making the reef colors less vibrant from the air and the water.
The rains taper off and the skies clear. Water visibility improves significantly, offering excellent views of the coral formations and the swirling sands of Whitehaven Beach.

The dry season offers the clearest skies and the best water visibility. The contrast between the deep blue ocean, the turquoise shallows, and the bright coral cays is at its sharpest, making this the best time for scenic flights and boat trips.
Humidity and temperatures begin to rise as the wet season approaches. The views remain strong, though occasional afternoon clouds and early rains can soften the light on the water.

gemini.depth_why: Visibility and access change with the Harmattan dust and the rainy seasons.
gemini.overview: Ghana's scenery is defined by its palm-fringed Atlantic coastline and dense tropical forests. Visitors can walk above the jungle canopy at Kakum National Park, look out over the ocean from the coastal forts of Cape Coast, and hike to Wli Waterfalls in the eastern highlands. The views are clearest and most accessible just after the rainy season.

blurbs.text: Harmattan winds blow in fine dust from the north, creating a haze that obscures long-distance views along the coast and in the eastern highlands.
The seasonal dust clears, restoring sharp views of the coastline and the forest canopy before the heaviest rains arrive.
Heavy seasonal rains swell the rivers and waterfalls, but frequent downpours and muddy unpaved roads complicate access to remote forest trails.
The landscape is lush and green from the recent rains, and clear skies provide sharp visibility for photographing the coast and hiking to the waterfalls.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise and fall with the opening and closing of the high-elevation roads.
gemini.overview: The region is defined by steep, glacially carved mountains and deep valleys filled with clear water. The Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses the Continental Divide at Logan Pass, providing access to high alpine viewpoints. Lower elevations feature dense forests and large, reflective bodies of water like Lake McDonald.

blurbs.text: Heavy snow closes most routes, including the higher elevations of the Going-to-the-Sun Road. Views are limited to the lower valleys and the frozen edges of Lake McDonald.
Lower elevations and valley roads open as the snowpack begins to melt. Waterfalls run high, though Logan Pass remains blocked by snow.
